Well, early on, early on, we ran into the problem that the officials of the union, of the unions, were in many ways totally ignorant of the music business, more so than me. And I was pretty dumb about it, okay? And so what they would do is they'd look up the rule book or call the international office, the national office of the union. It was in New Jersey in those days, I think. It may still be. And ask them, well, what about this or what about that? And the union would give them the religious answer, you know. And in other words, they wouldn't say what maybe they did in New York or L.A. or something like that. They'd say, oh, the rule says such and such. And so we would get these intensely stringent interpretations of the rules and sometimes misinterpretations of the rules. And they were handed down like Moses carrying the stone, you know. It was really difficult. And lots of things were just plain dumb. I remember once I was doing a session and they stopped us because the company I was recording was named Wings, but it was a division of Mercury. And Mercury was the signatory to the Musicians Performance Trust Fund, which you had to belong to and contribute to or they wouldn't let you use union musicians. And so they stopped the session because there was no Wings company listed on their list of people who were signatories.
Signatories, right.

And so after some long-distance calls and stuff like that and the wasting of a couple of hours, the representative of the union that was there was satisfied that Wings was a proper company to record. He says, yeah, but I was sent here with the authority to stop the session, not the authority to let it restart. And we had to then find the president of the local who was an insurance salesman, what's called industrial insurance, where they go house to house and they collect two bits a week on the burial policies and things like that. So this guy's out on his debit.
